extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claimed subject matter that recites a judicial exception is integrated into a practical application (Alice/Mayo Step 2A Prong Two), including when products of nature have 'markedly different characteristics'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly Different Characteristics (products of nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be 'markedly different' from its naturally occurring counterpart, a claimed product must possess at least one characteristic that is changed as compared to the counterpart; the characteristic cannot be an inherent or innate characteristic of the naturally occurring counterpart or an incidental change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require that the inventor caused the change. Examples of markedly different products: Chakrabarty (genetically modified bacterium with additional plasmids and expanded hydrocarbon degradation capability); Myriad (full-length cDNA with a different nucleotide sequence containing only exons). Anti-examples: mere isolation or incidental structural differences that leave the molecule otherwise identical (Myriad's isolated BRCA genes), single-stranded primers whose sequences are identical to natural strands (Ambry), clones that are genetic replicas (Roslin). Cite Myriad, Chakrabarty, Ambry Genetics, In re Roslin, and In re Marden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-of-nature exception applies when no marked difference
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is no change in any characteristic between the claimed product and its natural counterpart, the claimed product lacks markedly different characteristics and is a product of nature exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isolation that only removes covalent bonds but leaves genetic structure and nucleotide sequence identical is insufficient (Myriad). Changes that are incidental or innate to the natural material do not avoid the exception. Courts consider whether patented claims would improperly tie up future use and study of the natural material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration into a Practical Application (Step 2A Prong Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: After determining a claim recites a judicial exception (Step 2A Prong One), determine whether the claim as a whole integrates the judicial exception into a practical application; if it does, the claim is not directed to the judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B; if it does not, further analysis under Step 2B is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim 'integrates' the exception when the additional elements apply, rely on, or use the exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception such that the claim is more than a drafting effort to monopolize the exception. Evaluate additional elements individually and in combination using the listed considerations. The analysis is claim-specific (each claim examined separately). Examples: Solutran (claims did not integrate; were directed to abstract idea); Finjan (security profile improvements integrated exception and were eligible). See MPEP § 2106 flowchart and §§ 2106.05 for Step 2B connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerations indicative that additional elements may integrate the exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations the courts have found indicative that an additional element (or combination of elements) may have integrated the exception into a practical application include: improvements in functioning of a computer or other technology; applying/using the exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis; implementing/using the exception with a particular machine or manufacture integral to the claim; effecting a transformation or reduction of an article to a different state or thing; applying/using the exception in some other meaningful way beyond generally linking it to a technological environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This list is not exclusive or limiting; additional elements can be analyzed based on more than one consideration. See MPEP §§ 2106.04(d)(1), 2106.04(d)(2), and 2106.05(a)-(h) for detailed treatment and examples (Enfish, McRO, Visual Memory, Finjan, SRI, BASCOM).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations that did not integrate a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations the courts have found did not integrate the judicial exception include: merely reciting 'apply it' (or equivalent) with the judicial exception, merely including instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer, or merely using a computer as a tool; adding insignificant extra-solution activity to the exception; generally linking the use of the exception to a particular technological environment or field of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such limitations are insufficient to impose a meaningful limit and often result in the claim being directed to the judicial exception. See MPEP §§ 2106.05(f)-(h) and cases like Alice and Bilski for context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give weight to all additional elements, including conventional ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should give weight to all additional elements, whether or not they are conventional, when evaluating whether a judicial exception has been integrated into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional elements that represent well-understood, routine, conventional activity may nevertheless integrate the exception into a practical application. Do not ignore conventional features in Step 2A Prong Two. Note that mere physicality or tangibility of an additional element is not a relevant consideration (Alice: physical implementation alone does not guarantee eligibility), nor is non-physicality necessarily fatal (Enfish, McRO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of a method of achieving a result is not a stand-alone consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific way of achieving a result is not itself a stand-alone consideration in Step 2A Prong Two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, specificity of limitations is relevant to evaluation of other considerations such as use of a particular machine, particular transformation, or whether limitations are mere instructions to apply an exception. Example: Parker v. Flook—failure to explain specifics of how to use a claimed formula informed the court that additional elements were insignificant post-solution activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for evaluating integration (how to evaluate additional elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate integration into a practical application by: (1) identifying whether there are additional elements recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s); and (2) evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they integrate the exception into a practical application using one or more of the relevant considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all considerations will be relevant to every claim. The evaluation is not a weighing test; it is important to evaluate the significance of the additional elements relative to the invention and whether the exception is integrated. If the claim as a whole integrates the exception based on these considerations, the additional limitations impose a meaningful limit and the claim is eligible at Step 2A. For multi-exception claims, see MPEP § 2106 subsection II.B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating improvements in computer functioning or other technology (Step 2A)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim reciting a judicial exception is not directed to the exception if it recites additional elements demonstrating the claimed invention improves the functioning of a computer or another technology or technical field; using the exception in this manner meaningfully limits the claim and transforms it into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evaluate, first review the specification to determine if the disclosure provides sufficient details such that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement. The specification need not explicitly assert the improvement, but the improvement must be apparent to a POSITA. Second, ensure the claim includes the components or steps that provide the improvement; the claim need not explicitly recite the improvement. This Step 2A improvements analysis differs from Step 2B analysis because it does not reference whether elements are well-understood, routine, conventional. Examples of eligible improvements include Enfish (self-referential table), McRO (automatic lip-sync), Visual Memory (enhanced memory system), Finjan (virus scanning that improves functionality). See MPEP § 2106.05(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular treatment or prophylaxis as an integrating consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying or using a judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition can integrate the exception into a practical application and render the claim not directed to the judicial exception (eligible at Step 2A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originated from 'other meaningful limitations' consideration and elevated due to cases like Vanda. Examples include administration of medication, surgery, dialysis, phototherapy, immunization steps that lower risk. The limitation must affirmatively recite an action of treatment or prophylaxis (e.g., 'administering amazonic acid to a patient'); mere statements of intended use, field-of-use, or non-affirmative recitations (e.g., 'prescribing' or 'a pharmaceutical composition') do not qualify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity vs. Generality of Treatment/Prophylaxis
rubrics_metrics.description: A treatment or prophylaxis limitation must be 'particular'—specifically identified so that it does not encompass all applications of the judicial exception—in order to integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'administering a lower than normal dosage of a beta blocker to a patient identified as a poor metabolizer' is particular and integrates a mental-analysis step into a practical application; by contrast, 'administering a suitable medication to a patient' is generic and merely instructs application of the exception. Examiners may consider overlap with mere-instruction, field-of-use, and other considerations when assessing particularity (see MPEP §§ 2106.05(f), 2106.05(h)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether limitation(s) have more than a nominal or insignificant relationship to the exception
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether a claim uses a recited judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis, assess whether the treatment/prophylaxis limitation has more than a nominal or insignificant relationship to the exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vanda contrasted with Mayo: Vanda's administration steps used the law of nature to safely treat patients (reducing risk), whereas Mayo's administration step was ancillary and performed to gather data about the law of nature. Thus, the relationship must be substantive (not ancillary or merely for data gathering) so the limitation meaningfully applies the exception rather than being ancillary to a diagnostic focus. Consider particularity and the role the limitation plays relative to the exception when making this determination.
